summary: Presents a framework to help the writers of certificate policies or certification practice statements for certification authorities and PKIs. It lists topics that may need covering. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 3647.

plainLanguage.summary: A company that issues digital ID cards has to write down its rules. This document is a checklist of what those rulebooks should cover.

questions: what is a certification practice statement
subtitle: A checklist for writing rules about how digital certificates are issued and managed.

tldr.problem: Certification authorities issuing digital certificates needed to write down their practices, but there was no standard framework for what topics to cover in these documents, risking incomplete or inconsistent policies.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2527 provides a comprehensive framework with eight major components and many subcomponents covering everything from legal obligations to technical security controls, creating a checklist for CA policy writers.
tldr.outcome: Certificate authorities can now write complete, comparable policies using this framework as a guide. The RFC was replaced by RFC 3647 with refinements.

today: RFC 3647 supersedes this RFC with refinements and clarifications based on experience implementing RFC 2527 frameworks.

sections.title: The Framework Purpose
sections.content:
When a certification authority (CA) issues a digital certificate, it is binding a public key to an entity's identity. But how much should you trust that binding? That depends on the CA's practices: how thoroughly it authenticated the applicant, how securely it protects its keys, what legal obligations it accepts.

RFC 2527 presents a framework to help CA writers document these practices. It is not a specific policy or a standard—instead, it is a checklist of topics that the writer should consider addressing. A certificate policy is a brief, high-level statement of rules that might apply to multiple CAs. A certification practice statement (CPS) is a detailed description by one CA of its own practices. Both can use this framework.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC is a master checklist for companies writing down their rules about digital certificates. It helps them remember what topics to cover.

sections.title: General Provisions: Legal and Liability Topics
sections.content:
The framework starts with legal and general topics: obligations (what the CA, repositories, registration authorities, subscribers, and relying parties must do), liability (warranties, damages caps, exclusions), financial responsibility (indemnification, fiduciary duties), interpretation and enforcement (governing law, dispute resolution), fees, publication, compliance audit, confidentiality, and intellectual property rights.

For example, a CPS must state whether the CA guarantees the accuracy of the identities it certifies, whether it limits its liability to the value of a certificate, what circumstances permit disclosure of confidential information, and how disputes are resolved.
sections.plainLanguage: The first section is about legal promises and rules: what the CA and others must do, what happens if something goes wrong, and how much money the CA will pay if it makes a mistake.

sections.title: Identification, Authentication, and Operational Controls
sections.content:
The framework describes how to authenticate applicants for certificates: what names are allowed, whether they must be unique, how disputes are resolved, what evidence of identity is required. It covers routine rekey (getting a new certificate), rekey after revocation, and how to authenticate revocation requests.

The operational requirements section details the entire certificate lifecycle: how applications are submitted, how certificates are issued and accepted, when certificates are suspended or revoked, how long revocation information is kept, whether revocation checking is required. It also covers record archival, disaster recovery, and termination procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: This section covers who can get a certificate (and what proof they must show), what happens as the certificate is issued and used, and what happens if something is compromised or the company shuts down.

sections.title: Physical and Personnel Security Controls
sections.content:
The framework requires CAs to describe their physical security: where the facility is located, who can access it, power and air conditioning, fire protection, media storage, waste disposal, and off-site backup. It also covers procedural controls: who has which trusted roles and how many people are needed to perform sensitive tasks (the n out of m rule, where two people must approve a key activation).

Personnel security is critical: background checks for staff in trusted roles, training and retraining, job rotation, sanctions for misconduct, contracting rules, and bonding. These non-technical controls are as important as any algorithm, because a CA's key is worthless if an insider can steal it.
sections.plainLanguage: This covers how the company physically protects its computers and keys from theft or damage, and what kind of people it hires and how it trusts them.

sections.title: Technical and Cryptographic Security
sections.content:
The framework covers technical controls: how cryptographic keys are generated, who generates them, where they are stored (in hardware or software), and how the private key is protected. Key questions include: Is the key under multi-person control? Is it escrowed? Backed up? Archived? Who can use it and how is it activated and deactivated?

The framework also addresses activation data (PINs, passwords, manually-held key shares), computer security controls (access controls, auditing), life-cycle security (how software is developed and maintained), network security (firewalls), and cryptographic module engineering (standards like FIPS 140-1). The goal is to ensure that all secret keys and critical parameters are protected throughout their lifecycle.
sections.plainLanguage: This covers how the company generates and protects its secret keys, who can use them and when, and what computer and network protections are in place.

sections.title: Certificate Profiles and Specification Administration
sections.content:
The framework specifies how to describe the certificate format: which X.509 extensions are populated, what cryptographic algorithms are used, what names are permitted, which certificate policy identifiers apply, and how the certificate policy extension is processed. Similar details apply to certificate revocation lists (CRLs) if used.

Finally, the framework covers how the policy itself is maintained: how changes are made (and whether they require a new policy identifier), how the policy is published and notification procedures for changes, and how CPSs are approved. A change that weakens security requires a new policy identifier, while a clarification may not.
sections.plainLanguage: This covers what information goes inside a digital certificate, and how the policy document itself is kept up to date when the company's practices change.
